statement_en: Let $p(x)\in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ with positive leading coefficient. Is it true that\[A=\{ p(n)+1/n : n\in \mathbb{N}\}\]is strongly complete, in the sense that, for any finite set $B$,\[\left\{\sum_{n\in X}n : X\subseteq A\backslash B\textrm{ finite }\right\}\]contains all sufficiently large integers?
source: google-deepmind/formal-conjectures@077138338750 FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/351.lean (main theorem; answer stripped; comments removed; identity renamed)

issues: Domain restriction: A only requires p ∈ Q[x] to have a positive leading coefficient, which literally includes nonzero constant polynomials p = c > 0 (degree 0). B adds the hypothesis deg P ≥ 1, so a proof of B leaves the constant case A = {c + 1/n} unaddressed. That case is not obviously trivial: it amounts to representing every large integer as k·c plus a sum of k distinct unit fractions, avoiding finitely many excluded ones.

Minor, harmless: B includes n = 0 with the convention 1/0 = 0, adding the extra value P(0). Because B quantifies over all finite excluded sets, one can take B ∪ {P(0)}. This gives A_orig \ B ⊇ A_B \ (B ∪ {P(0)}), so B for all finite sets still implies A's conclusion.
Otherwise the rest matches: distinct elements of the value set, every finite removal set, and all sufficiently large naturals.
faithfulness.verdict: B proves the conjecture only for polynomials of degree ≥ 1, while A as literally stated also covers positive constant polynomials, so B is a strict weakening and would not fully settle A's `pos` direction.
faithfulness.backtranslation:
**Statement.** Let $P$ be any polynomial with rational coefficients, of degree at least $1$ and with positive leading coefficient. Let $A$ be the set of rational numbers
$$A = \{\, P(n) + 1/n : n = 0, 1, 2, \dots \,\},$$
with the convention $1/0 = 0$, so $n = 0$ contributes the value $P(0)$. The claim is that for every finite set $B$ of rational numbers, there is a threshold $M$ such that every natural number $m \ge M$ is the sum of the elements of some finite subset of $A \setminus B$.

Here "finite subset" means a sum of distinct elements of the value set, so each value is used at most once. Equivalently, $A$ is "strongly complete": after removing any finitely many elements, every sufficiently large integer is still a finite sum of distinct remaining elements.
